title: How would you design AI inference infra with GPU queue and KV-cache?
description: Design a scalable LLM inference platform handling bursty traffic, GPU scheduling, and KV-cache reuse.
answer:
Front a stateless API with a **GPU-aware queue** (continuous batching), cache **KV blocks by prefix** (RadixAttention/pagedAttention), and autoscale GPU pods on queue depth + TTFT SLO — not CPU.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Client -> GPU queue (continuous batch) -> paged KV-cache -> token stream</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">API + Queue</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">FIFO + priority</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">queue depth SLO</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">backpressure 429</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Scheduler</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">continuous batching</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">pagedAttention</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">prefix reuse</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">GPU Pool</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">KV blocks shared</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">HBM bound</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">scale on TTFT</text></svg>

**Architecture.** Clients hit an **inference gateway** that validates, tokenizes, and enqueues by priority (interactive > batch). A **GPU scheduler** (vLLM/TensorRT-LLM style) does **continuous batching**: as soon as one request finishes decoding a token, the next queued request fills the slot — no waiting for whole-batch completion. **Paged KV-cache** stores key/value blocks in non-contiguous HBM pages and shares prefix blocks across requests (`system prompt + few-shot`); a **Radix tree** indexes prefixes so a hit reuses compute and cuts TTFT 40-70%. Scale **GPU replicas** on `p95 TTFT` and queue depth; keep **CPU prefill** separate from decode where possible. Persist prompts/results to object storage for retries and eval.

| Decision | Choice | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Batching | continuous > static | 3-5x throughput, lower tail latency |
| KV-cache | paged + prefix tree | reuse system prompt, save HBM |
| Queue | priority + max tokens | interactive SLO vs batch throughput |
| Scaling signal | TTFT + queue depth | CPU is irrelevant for GPUs |

> **Interview tip:** Sketch the **prefill vs decode** split, mention **pagedAttention** and **prefix cache hit rate** as the metric, and say you autoscale on **TTFT p95**, not GPU util — interviewers love that.

```python
# pseudo: prefix-aware scheduler (vLLM style)
from radix import RadixCache
cache = RadixCache()

def schedule(req):
    prefix_hit, blocks = cache.match(req.tokens)  # reuse KV
    # continuous batching: insert into running batch if HBM fits
    if gpu.free_blocks() >= blocks_needed(req) - prefix_hit:
        batch.add(req, shared_blocks=blocks)
    else:
        queue.enqueue(req, priority=req.slo)

# prometheus: histogram TTFT, queue_depth, kv_hit_ratio
```

title: What is KV-cache and how does prefix caching speed up LLM inference?
description: Explain pagedAttention, KV-cache memory math, and prefix/Radix caching.
answer:
**KV-cache** stores per-token **Key/Value** projections so decode is O(1) per token; **prefix caching** reuses those blocks across requests sharing a prefix (system prompt/tools), saving prefill compute and HBM.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Without cache O(n^2) -> with KV O(n) -> prefix reuse = 0 prefill for hit</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">No cache</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">recompute K/V each token</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">O(n^2) attention</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">HBM thrash</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">KV-cache</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">store K/V per token</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">decode O(1)</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">HBM = 2*len*layers</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Prefix cache</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">Radix tree lookup</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">hit = skip prefill</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">40-70% TTFT cut</text></svg>

**How it works.** Each transformer layer projects tokens to K/V. Without cache, generating token *n* recomputes K/V for 1..n-1. **KV-cache** persists them. Memory ~ `2 x tokens x layers x hidden x bytes` — e.g., 8k tokens on a 70B can be ~10 GB, so **pagedAttention** splits cache into fixed-size blocks (like OS pages) to avoid fragmentation. **Prefix caching** hashes the token prefix; a shared `You are helpful... + tools` prefix across thousands of requests is computed once and **reference-counted**. Advanced: **chunked prefill** to bound latency, and **quantized KV** (int8) to double capacity.

| Technique | Saves | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| KV-cache | compute | HBM capacity |
| Paged blocks | fragmentation | block table |
| Prefix/Radix | prefill latency | cache invalidation on model change |
| KV quant int8 | 2x capacity | small quality loss |

> **Interview tip:** Do the **HBM math** on the board: `2 * seq_len * layers * dim * 2 bytes` and show when you OOM — then offer **paged + eviction** as the fix; it signals you have shipped inference.

```python
def kv_memory_gb(seq_len, n_layers=80, d_model=8192, bytes_per=2):
    return 2 * seq_len * n_layers * d_model * bytes_per / 1e9

print(kv_memory_gb(8192))  # ~10.7 GB for 70B-like

# Radix lookup pseudo
node = radix_root.longest_prefix_match(tokens)
if node.hit_ratio > 0.5:
    reuse_blocks(node.kv_blocks)
else:
    prefill(tokens)
```

title: Kafka vs SQS — how do you choose for an event-driven system in 2025?
description: Compare throughput, ordering, replay, and ops for event streaming.
answer:
**Kafka** = ordered log, replay, high throughput, you operate it; **SQS** = serverless queue, at-least-once, no replay, scales to zero — pick Kafka for streaming/analytics, SQS for decoupled jobs.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Producer -> Kafka (log, partitions) <-> SQS (queue, visibility timeout) -> Consumer</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Kafka</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">partitioned log</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">replay + retention</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">ordering per key</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">SQS Standard</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">no ordering</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">at-least-once</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">infinite scale</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">SQS FIFO</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">ordering per group</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">exactly-once dedupe</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">300 TPS/group</text></svg>

**Deep compare.** **Kafka** persists an **append-only log per partition** with retention (days), consumers track offsets — you can **replay** from any offset, do stream processing (Kafka Streams/Flink), and get **strict order per partition key**. Throughput ~ millions/s but you manage brokers, partitioning, and rebalances. **SQS** is fully managed: **Standard** offers best-effort ordering + **at-least-once** with **visibility timeout**; **FIFO** adds ordering per `MessageGroupId` + **deduplication ID** for effectively-once, capped at ~300 TPS per group (batch 3k). No replay — need DLQ for poison. In 2025 mix: **Kafka for event sourcing/streaming**, **SQS (+SNS/EventBridge)** for job queues and fan-out where serverless matters.

| Criterion | Kafka | SQS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replay | yes (offset rewind) | no (DLQ only) |
| Ordering | per partition key | FIFO group only |
| Throughput | M/s per cluster | auto, FIFO limited |
| Ops | brokers, ZooKeeper/KRaft | serverless |
| Use | streams, CDC, analytics | jobs, decoupling |

> **Interview tip:** Start with **do you need replay?** — if yes, Kafka wins automatically; if **at-least-once is fine and you want zero ops**, SQS. Mention **Kinesis vs MSK** as AWS-managed Kafka.

```python
# idempotent consumer — works for both
import boto3, hashlib
seen = set()  # use Redis/dynamo in prod

def handle(msg):
    dedup = hashlib.sha256(msg.body.encode()).hexdigest()
    if dedup in seen: return  # exactly-once effect
    process(msg.body)
    seen.add(dedup)
    msg.delete()  # SQS: delete; Kafka: commit offset

# SQS FIFO send
sqs.send_message(QueueUrl=url, MessageBody='order:1',
    MessageGroupId='user-42', MessageDeduplicationId=dedup)
```

title: Exactly-once processing — can Kafka or SQS guarantee it?
description: Idempotency, transactions, and outbox for true exactly-once effects.
answer:
Neither guarantees **exactly-once effects** end-to-end; Kafka gives **exactly-once within Kafka** (transactions + idempotent producer), but your side-effects need **idempotency keys + dedupe store**.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Produce idempotent -> Kafka txn -> consume -> idempotent handler -> dedupe DB</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Kafka EOS</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">txn + idempotent</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">within cluster</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">needs app idempotence</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">SQS</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">at-least-once</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">visibility timeout</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">DLQ + dedupe</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">App fix</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">idempotency key</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">exactly-once effect</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">store key+result</text></svg>

**How it works.** **Kafka EOS** uses `enable.idempotence + transactional.id` to avoid dup writes and atomic `send + offset commit` (`transactional` consumer). But if your handler calls Stripe or writes DB, a crash after Stripe but before commit still dupes — so add **idempotency key** (e.g., `event_id`) stored in a **dedupe table** with unique constraint; insert-or-ignore before side-effect. For **SQS**, dupes come from retries/visibility timeout expiry — same pattern: check dedupe store first, use **FIFO + ContentBasedDedup** to reduce but still guard. The **outbox pattern** (write event + business row in one DB txn, then relay) gives atomic publish without 2PC.

| Layer | Guarantee | What remains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kafka producer | exactly-once to topic | consumer dupes still possible |
| Kafka txn | atomic offsets+records | external calls not covered |
| SQS FIFO | dedup 5min window | beyond 5min dupes |
| App idempotency | end-to-end once | needs dedupe store TTL |

> **Interview tip:** Say **exactly-once = idempotent producer + transactional offsets + idempotent consumer** — never claim the broker alone solves it; interviewers test that nuance.

```sql
-- dedupe table for exactly-once effect
CREATE TABLE processed (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, result JSONB, created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());
-- handler
INSERT INTO processed(id, result) VALUES (:event_id, :result)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING RETURNING *;
-- if row inserted, do side-effect; else return stored result
```

title: Head vs tail sampling in OpenTelemetry — when does each break?
description: Sampling strategies, cost, and tail-based decision with Collector.
answer:
**Head sampling** decides at creation (cheap, blind); **tail sampling** decides after seeing latency/error (smart, costly) — production uses **head 1-5% + tail keeps all errors/slow**.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">SDK head 1% -> Collector buffer 10s -> tail: keep error/slow/1% ok</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Head</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">at SDK start</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">random 1%</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">misses needle</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Tail</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">after response</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">keep p99 + 5xx</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">needs memory</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Hybrid</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">head 5% + tail</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">best cost/signal</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">most prod</text></svg>

**How it works.** **Head** (`parentbased_traceidratio 0.01`) drops before you know if it's interesting — cheap, but you lose the one error in 10k. **Tail** buffers spans in the **Collector** (`tail_sampling` processor) for e.g., 10s, then decides: `status_code==ERROR OR duration > 1s OR probabilistic 1%`. Keeps 100% of useful signal but needs RAM to buffer and adds latency. **Hybrid** starts with low head to cut volume, then tail upgrades. In **Kafka** propagation, pass `traceparent` as header so consumer span links. Always emit **metrics (histograms) unsampled** — traces are for drill-down, not counting.

| Strategy | Useful trace kept | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head 1% | 1% random | lowest |
| Tail 100% errors | 100% errors | medium RAM |
| Hybrid | 100% errors + 1% ok | balanced |
| No sampling | 100% | highest |

> **Interview tip:** Draw the **Collector pipeline** (`receiver -> batch -> tail_sampling -> exporter`) and say **metrics stay unsampled** — it shows you won't lose SLO counts.

```yaml
# otel-collector tail sampling
processors:
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]}
      - name: slow
        type: latency
        latency: {threshold_ms: 1000}
      - name: probabilistic
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: {sampling_percentage: 1}
```

title: How do you build a sliding-window rate limiter with Redis + Lua?
description: Atomic fixed vs sliding window, Lua script, and distributed correctness.
answer:
Use a **sorted set per key** + **Lua atomic** `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE + ZCARD + ZADD`: window = now- N sec, count, allow if < limit — single round-trip, race-free.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Request -> Lua: ZREMRANGE old -> ZCARD -> if < limit ZADD now -> allow/429</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Fixed window</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">bucket per minute</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">burst at edge</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">2x at boundary</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Sliding window</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">sorted set + Lua</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">smooth, precise</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">1 Lua RTT</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Token bucket</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">refill per sec</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">burst ok</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">needs refill calc</text></svg>

**How it works.** Store timestamps in a **Redis Sorted Set** (`key = user:42`, score = epoch ms). Lua does atomically: `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key 0 now-window`, `ZCARD`, if `count < limit` then `ZADD key now now + EXPIRE`, return allow; else return `retry_after = oldest + window - now`. This is **precise sliding window** (not leaky fixed). Single Lua execution is atomic (no race across 10 API pods). **In-memory alternative** fails distributed; per-node limits drift. Add **partition key** `user:42:2025-08-26` to bound set size, and `PEXPIRE` to auto-GC. For **burst**, add token bucket layer; for **global**, shard by `userId` to one Redis cluster or use **Redis Cell** module.

| Algorithm | Precision | Burst | Implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed window | coarse | 2x at boundary | INCR+EXPIRE |
| Sliding window | exact | no | Lua ZSET |
| Token bucket | smooth | yes | Lua + refill |
| Leaky bucket | smooth | no | queue |

> **Interview tip:** Write the **Lua 5-liner** on the board — interviewers check for **atomicity** (Lua) and mention **2x burst** of fixed window as why you chose sliding.

```lua
-- sliding_window.lua KEYS[1] ARGV[1]=window_ms ARGV[2]=limit ARGV[3]=now
local key, window, limit, now = KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, now - window)
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', key)
if count < limit then
  redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now .. ':' .. math.random())
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window)
  return {1, limit - count - 1}
else
  local oldest = redis.call('ZRANGE', key, 0, 0, 'WITHSCORES')
  return {0, tonumber(oldest[2]) + window - now}
end
```

title: Token bucket vs sliding window vs fixed window — which rate limiter when?
description: Choose the right algorithm per product need: burst, smoothness, precision.
answer:
**Fixed window** = simple but 2x burst at boundary; **sliding window** = precise, no burst; **token bucket** = allows burst up to bucket size — API gateways use **token bucket**, abuse prevention uses **sliding window**.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Fixed 2x burst -> Sliding smooth cap -> Token burst+refill</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Fixed</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">INCR per window</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">2x at edge</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">cheapest</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Sliding</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">Lua ZSET</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">precise cap</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">accurate abuse</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Token bucket</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">tokens refill/sec</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">burst allowed</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">API UX best</text></svg>

**How to choose.** **Fixed window** (`INCR key; EXPIRE 60`) is cheapest but allows `limit` at `00:59` + `limit` at `01:00` = 2x. **Sliding window** (Lua ZSET) fixes that — every request checked against last N seconds, no burst, perfect for **login/OTP** abuse caps. **Token bucket** (`tokens += refill_rate * delta, cap at burst`) allows **burst** then throttles to sustained rate — best for **API gateways** where clients retry and UX matters (Stripe, GitHub). For **distributed**, all three must be **Redis/Lua** or **Envoy local + global** hybrid; per-process counters drift 10x under load.

| Use case | Best algorithm | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Login/OTP | sliding window | no 2x burst |
| Public API | token bucket | burst for retries |
| Cheap internal | fixed window | simple, low precision ok |
| Scheduler | leaky bucket | smooth output rate |

> **Interview tip:** Say **Stripe uses token bucket** for burst-friendly APIs, **auth uses sliding window** — naming a real product's choice is the senior signal.

```python
import time, redis
r = redis.Redis()
BUCKET, REFILL, CAP = 'api:uid', 10, 50  # 10/s, burst 50
def allow(uid):
    lua = """
    local tokens = tonumber(redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) or ARGV[2])
    local last = tonumber(redis.call('get', KEYS[2]) or ARGV[3])
    local now, refill = tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[1])
    tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[2]), tokens + (now-last)*refill)
    if tokens >= 1 then redis.call('set', KEYS[1], tokens-1); redis.call('set', KEYS[2], now); return 1 else redis.call('set', KEYS[1], tokens); redis.call('set', KEYS[2], now); return 0 end"""
    return r.eval(lua, 2, f'{BUCKET}:{uid}', f'{BUCKET}:{uid}:ts', REFILL, CAP, time.time())
```

title: What is consistent hashing with virtual nodes and when do you need it?
description: Ring, virtual nodes, and rebalancing without full reshuffle.
answer:
Map **nodes + keys** to a **hash ring**; a key belongs to the next clockwise node — adding a node moves only `1/N` keys. **Virtual nodes** (100-200 per physical) smooth skew.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Keys + Nodes on ring -> clockwise owner -> vnodes for balance -> 1/N move on change</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Naive mod</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">key % N</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">all move on N up</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">unusable</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Ring</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">hash ring</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">K/N moves</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">minimal</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Vnodes</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">150 per node</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">stddev <10%</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">balanced</text></svg>

**How it works.** Hash both **node IDs** and **keys** into e.g., `0..2^32-1` sorted ring; walk clockwise to find owner. Adding node 5 to a 4-node ring moves only keys between its predecessor and it (~1/5). **Virtual nodes** replicate each physical node 150x at random ring positions — balances load when nodes differ in capacity (give bigger nodes more vnodes) and when `N` is small (otherwise one node owns 70%). Used in **Dynamo, Cassandra, CDN, distributed cache** (memcached) and **sharded queues**. Alternatives: **rendezvous (HRW)** hashes `hash(key, node)` and picks max — simpler for small N, no ring.

| Scheme | Keys moved on +1 node | Balance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mod N | ~100% | worst |
| consistent | 1/(N+1) | ok, needs vnodes |
| vnodes 150 | 1/(N+1) | excellent |
| rendezvous | 1/(N+1) | good, O(N) lookup |

> **Interview tip:** Draw the **ring with vnodes** and say **give heavy nodes more vnodes** — it answers the follow-up 'heterogeneous hardware?' instantly.

```python
import hashlib, bisect
class Ring:
    def __init__(self, nodes, v=150):
        self.ring=[]; self.map={}
        for n in nodes:
            for i in range(v):
                h=int(hashlib.md5(f'{n}#{i}'.encode()).hexdigest(),16)
                self.ring.append(h); self.map[h]=n
        self.ring.sort()
    def owner(self, key):
        h=int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(),16)
        idx=bisect.bisect(self.ring, h)%len(self.ring)
        return self.map[self.ring[idx]]
```

title: Consistent hashing vs rendezvous (HRW) hashing — which for what scale?
description: Tradeoff: ring with vnodes vs highest-weight node per key.
answer:
**Rendezvous**: compute `hash(key, node)` for every node, pick max — O(N) but perfect balance, no ring. **Consistent hashing**: O(log N) ring, needs vnodes — better for 100+ nodes.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">HRW O(N) max-hash -> Consistent O(log N) ring -> picks per N size</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Rendezvous</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">hash(k,n) per node</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">O(N) lookup</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">perfect balance</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Consistent</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">ring + vnodes</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">O(log N)</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">needs vnodes</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Rule</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">N < 50 -> HRW</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">N > 100 -> ring</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">both 1/N move</text></svg>

**How it works.** **HRW** is simpler: `score = hash(key + node_id)`, owner = `argmax score`. No ring, no vnodes, naturally uniform, trivial weighted variant (`score * weight`). Lookup is O(N) — fine for <50 cache nodes or weighted routing (Nginx HRW). **Consistent hashing** is O(log N) via binary search on ring, better for **Dynamo/Cassandra-scale** (100s nodes) and incremental join. Both move 1/(N+1) keys on membership change. In 2025, **CDN edge selection** often uses HRW (e.g., Cloudflare tiered), **storage sharding** uses consistent ring.

| Property | HRW | Consistent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lookup | O(N) | O(log N) |
| Balance | perfect | needs 150 vnodes |
| Weighted | multiply score | more vnodes |
| Simplicity | highest | ring infra |

> **Interview tip:** Say **HRW for CDN tier selection, ring for data sharding** — it shows you pick by N and lookup cost, not dogma.

```python
import hashlib
def rendezvous_owner(key, nodes):
    def score(n): return int(hashlib.md5(f'{key}|{n}'.encode()).hexdigest(),16)
    return max(nodes, key=score)
# weighted
def weighted_owner(key, nodes, weights):
    def wscore(n): return int(hashlib.md5(f'{key}|{n}'.encode()).hexdigest(),16) * weights[n]
    return max(nodes, key=wscore)
```

title: How does CDC with Debezium keep search and cache in sync with Postgres?
description: Log-based CDC, outbox vs WAL, ordering, and snapshot.
answer:
**Debezium** tails **Postgres WAL** (logical decoding) and publishes row changes to **Kafka** per table/topic — downstream consumers tail Kafka for **ordered, replayable, filtered** CDC without polling.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Postgres WAL -> Debezium -> Kafka (per-table) -> search/cache consumers</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">WAL tail</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">logical decoding</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">no app change</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">ordered</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Snapshot</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">initial dump</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">then stream</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">consistent</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Sink</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">Kafka -> ES/Redis</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">ordered per key</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">replayable</text></svg>

**How it works.** Enable `wal_level=logical`, create `publication`, Debezium connector reads **write-ahead log** and emits `before/after` envelopes to **Kafka** topics (`db.server.table`). On first run it **snapshots** existing rows then streams deltas. Consumers (Elasticsearch sink, Redis invalidator) use **Kafka ordering per key** (table PK) to apply idempotently. Handle **schema evolution** via Schema Registry, **tombstones** for deletes, and **outbox pattern** if you need transactional `order + outbox` row (dual-write without 2PC). Backpressure via Kafka lag metrics; re-create slot after failure from last committed offset.

| Method | Impact on DB | Ordering | Ops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polling | query load, lag | none | simple |
| Trigger | per-row cost | yes | fragile |
| WAL CDC | near zero, log read | per-key order | slots, lag mon |
| Outbox+CDC | transactional | per aggregate | extra table |

> **Interview tip:** Mention **replication slot lag** as the alert (`pg_replication_slots.active=false` = stale) and that **updates emit before+after** — it handles the 'how do you get old value?' follow-up.

```json
// debezium postgres connector (snippet)
{
  "name": "pg-orders",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "database.hostname": "pg",
    "database.dbname": "shop",
    "topic.prefix": "shop",
    "table.include.list": "public.orders"
  }
}
// Kafka msg: {"before": null, "after": {"id": 42, "status": "paid"}, "op": "c"}
```

title: Outbox pattern vs polling for CDC — how do you avoid dual-write failure?
description: Transactional outbox, polling relay, and Debezium outbox event router.
answer:
**Outbox**: write **business row + outbox row in one DB txn**, a relay publishes outbox to Kafka — no dual-write race. Polling relays every 100ms; Debezium **outbox event router** is log-based (no poll).

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">App txn: order + outbox -> Relay (poll/WAL) -> Kafka -> consumers</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#22c55e" stroke="#22c55e"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Dual write</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">2 systems</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">race/failure</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">lost event</text><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#f59e0b" stroke="#f59e0b"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">Polling relay</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">SELECT outbox</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">100ms lag</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">simple</text><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Log outbox</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">Debezium router</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">WAL, no poll</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5">lowest lag</text></svg>

**How it works.** Naive `DB commit + Kafka send` can send but not commit (or vice versa). **Outbox** fixes it: `BEGIN; INSERT orders; INSERT outbox(event, payload); COMMIT;` — one atomic unit. A **polling relay** (`SELECT ... WHERE published=false LIMIT 100`) publishes to Kafka then marks published. **Debezium Outbox Event Router** does the same but tails WAL — no polling load and leverages ordering. Consumers must be **idempotent** (replay after relay restart). Add **unique (aggregate_id, version)** in outbox to deduplicate retries and a **cleanup job** to archive published rows.

| Pattern | Atomicity | DB load | Latency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dual write | none | low | low but unsafe |
| Polling outbox | txn atomic | poll qps | 100-500ms |
| WAL outbox | txn atomic | log tail | <100ms |

> **Interview tip:** Say **outbox makes Kafka publish transactional without 2PC** — the one sentence that signals senior distributed-systems thinking.

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders(id, amount) VALUES (42, 100);
INSERT INTO outbox(aggregate_id, type, payload)
VALUES (42, 'OrderCreated', '{"id":42}');
COMMIT;
-- relay: SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published=false ORDER BY id LIMIT 100;
-- then publish to Kafka and UPDATE outbox SET published=true WHERE id=?
```
